pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–11 years

- **Topic:** Controlling variables (planning enquiries)

- **Standards — UK (DfE Upper KS2 Working Scientifically):** the statutory programme requires pupils are taught to "plan different types of scientific enquiries to answer questions, including recognising and controlling variables where necessary" (verbatim). Non-statutory guidance adds that upper-KS2 pupils should "recognise when and how to set up comparative and fair tests and explain which variables need to be controlled and why." This is the central experimental-design skill of the primary phase.

- **Standards — US (NGSS SEP 3 Planning & Carrying Out Investigations):** the 3–5 progression is "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-ESS2-1, 4-PS3-2, 5-PS1-3, 5-PS1-4]"; the overarching practice framing asks students to decide "which variables should be treated as results or outputs, which should be treated as inputs and intentionally varied… and which should be controlled, or kept the same across trials." This topic (ages 9–11) sits at that 3–5 core and previews the 6–8 shift to naming independent/dependent variables.

- **Operational details:** The hub of the primary experimental-design spine (highest centrality in its band). Builds on setting up simple fair tests (prerequisites mt_qgb76wHN2X, mt_eoPcc4nrBE) and identifying patterns/using evidence (mt_CVywzrjT_c). Two linked competencies: (1) CHOOSING THE RIGHT ENQUIRY TYPE for a question — fair test, observing over time, pattern-seeking, identifying/classifying, or research — rather than defaulting to fair testing; and (2) within a fair test, INDEPENDENTLY identifying the variable to change (independent), the variable to measure (dependent), and the variables to control, and explaining WHY control matters for a valid result. Feeds forward to prediction-driven re-testing and KS3 hypothesis-led full design (dependents mt_5PgQB0QkWi, mt_Ae56umVlTT).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). A learner who can independently plan an investigation identifying the change/measure/control variables, choose an appropriate enquiry type for a given question, and explain why controlling variables is essential for a valid result has met the bar. Formal hypothesis wording, sample size and risk assessment are the KS3 tier (mt_Ae56umVlTT).
bestPractices: Teach enquiry-TYPE selection explicitly against the five named types, using questions that are NOT best answered by a fair test (e.g. 'how does the moon's shape change over a month?' → observing over time; 'do taller children have longer arms?' → pattern-seeking) so pupils stop reflexively reaching for a fair test (the AKSIS over-default).

Move pupils from teacher-set to self-planned: give the question and have them decide the variables and the enquiry type, then justify their choices — planning independence is the assessed step-up from earlier fair-testing.

Require the 'why control?' justification for each controlled variable ('we keep the water amount the same because otherwise we couldn't tell if temperature or water amount caused the change') — controlling variables is understood, not just listed.
Introduce the input/output/kept-same language (independent/dependent/control in child-friendly form) as a bridge to the KS3 vocabulary, without over-formalising at this age.
Use a planning proforma (question → enquiry type → variable to change → to measure → to control → prediction → how to record) so the full plan is visible before any doing.
keyRepresentations: A five-enquiry-type selector (fair test / observe over time / pattern-seek / classify / research) matched to question types
An independent – dependent – control variable planner (the formalising of change/measure/keep-the-same)
A planning proforma from question through to recording method
A 'which variables must we control, and why?' annotated set-up
A decision flow: what kind of question is this → which enquiry answers it best
commonMisconceptions: Defaulting to a fair test for every question, including ones better answered by observing over time, pattern-seeking, classifying or research (the AKSIS over-default persists into upper KS2).
Listing controlled variables without understanding why control is necessary — not connecting uncontrolled variables to invalid, uninterpretable results.
Confusing the independent (changed) and dependent (measured) variables, or thinking the thing you measure is something you set.
Believing 'more variables changed = a better/bigger experiment', missing that changing more than one destroys attribution.
Thinking planning is a formality to rush past, rather than the step that determines whether the results can answer the question at all.

learn.summary: For ages 9–11: pupils learn to plan scientific enquiries by choosing the right enquiry type for a question and, within a fair test, assigning each factor as the variable to change (independent), measure (dependent), or keep the same (control), and justifying why control makes a result valid. The central active experience is designing a plan and seeing how an uncontrolled variable makes a result impossible to interpret. Supporting activities assess variable roles and enquiry-type matching and probe pupils' justifications. Alternatives include categorisation-and-matching questions and a Socratic plan-interrogation; a labelled reference image is a scaffold only.

activities.title: Design the plan, then run it: make a confound wreck your experiment
feedback: When key variables are left uncontrolled: 'More than one thing differed here (light, water, AND pot size) — you can't tell which caused the change. Lock the others so only the light varies.'

When a learner changes several factors deliberately: 'Varying more things at once does not make a better test — with light, water and pot all different, no single cause can be pinned down. Change exactly one.'

When the plan isolates a single variable: 'Only light differs among the things you controlled now, so a growth difference can more fairly be linked to light — though plants vary naturally, so repeating with several plants makes the answer more trustworthy.'

When 'fair test' is chosen for 'How does the Moon's appearance change over a month?': 'Nothing is being compared under controlled conditions here — this question asks you to watch how the Moon looks change over time. Pick the enquiry type that matches the question.'
When asked why a specific control matters: 'Say which rival explanation keeping the pot size the same rules out — control exists to make the cause attributable, not just to tidy things up.'
activities.rationale: Planning with variable control is a generative design decision; letting a learner build a plan, run it, and see an uncontrolled variable undermine the result is intended to make the necessity of control concrete rather than stated. A live planner-and-runner with a type-selector lets the mismatch between question and enquiry type show itself. This is proposed to address the reported AKSIS over-default to fair testing, the belief that changing more variables makes a bigger experiment, and the common failure to connect uncontrolled variables to uninterpretable results.
sourceClaims: DfE Upper KS2 Working Scientifically requires planning different types of scientific enquiries to answer questions, including recognising and controlling variables where necessary; guidance adds pupils should explain which variables need controlling and why.

NGSS SEP 3 at grades 3-5 requires investigations that control variables, with the practice framing asking students to decide which variables are outputs, which are intentionally varied inputs, and which are controlled/kept the same across trials.
Primary pupils over-default to fair testing rather than selecting from the five enquiry types (observing over time, pattern seeking, classifying, comparative/fair testing, research).
learnerActions: Take a real question (e.g. 'Do plants grow taller with more sunlight?') and plan an investigation before doing anything.
Choose one enquiry type from the five: fair/comparative test, observing over time, pattern-seeking, classifying/identifying, or research.
Sort each factor into 'change' (the one input you vary), 'measure' (the output/result), and 'keep the same' (controls).

Run the plan. If you left factors uncontrolled — e.g. the sunny plant also got more water and a bigger pot — observe how the result comes back ambiguous: 'light, water and pot size all differed, so we can't say which caused the growth.'
Fix the plan by keeping every other factor you can the same so only one is changed, re-run, and compare how a cleaner plan gives an answer you can more fairly put down to that one change.
Notice that changing several factors at once does not make a 'bigger or better' experiment — it only destroys your ability to attribute the effect to any one cause.

Try a question that is NOT best answered by a fair test (e.g. 'How does the Moon's appearance (its phase) change over a month?') and see that choosing 'fair test' misfires — observing over time fits better.
activities.intendedInsight: Controlling variables is not a rote rule: it removes rival explanations so a difference in results can be attributed to the one thing you changed. Changing more than one factor does not make the experiment stronger — it makes the cause unknowable. Different questions need different enquiry types, so a fair test is not always the right tool.

activities.title: Sort the variables and match the enquiry type
feedback: If independent and dependent are swapped: 'You set the amount of light; you measure the height. The thing you measure is an outcome, not something you choose.'
If a control is listed without reason: 'Which alternative explanation would differ if you did NOT keep this the same? That's why it's controlled.'

If every question is matched to 'fair test': 'Check whether the question compares conditions, watches change over time, looks for a pattern, sorts things into groups, or needs looking up — match the type to the question.'
activities.rationale: Matching questions to enquiry types, assigning variable roles, and justifying control map onto categorisation and multiple-choice formats, which can check and consolidate the planning evidence statements. This format assesses understanding but does not itself let a learner run their own flawed plan and see the consequence, so it complements rather than replaces the design-and-run activity.
sourceClaims: Primary pupils over-default to fair testing rather than selecting from the five enquiry types (observing over time, pattern seeking, classifying, comparative/fair testing, research).
learnerActions: Categorise a list of factors in a given investigation into independent (change), dependent (measure), and control (keep the same) roles.
Match several questions to their best-fitting enquiry type among the five named types.
Answer 'why must we keep X the same?' by naming the rival explanation it rules out.
activities.intendedInsight: Pupils can distinguish the thing you set from the thing you measure, and can pick an enquiry type fit to the question — the knowledge that underpins independent planning.

activities.title: Interrogate the plan: what else might be affecting your result?
feedback: If a hidden confound is missed: 'You changed the light, but did the two plants also start at different heights? Name every way they differ.'
If the justification is a bare rule: 'Keeping the pot size the same removes which possible cause? Tie the control to the explanation it eliminates.'
activities.rationale: A Socratic interrogation exercises the justification skill and probes for hidden uncontrolled variables and wrong enquiry-type choices. It pairs well AFTER the design-and-run planner, but on its own does not execute the investigation to show whether the plan is valid, so it is a complement rather than the primary teach.
sourceClaims: DfE Upper KS2 Working Scientifically requires planning different types of scientific enquiries to answer questions, including recognising and controlling variables where necessary; guidance adds pupils should explain which variables need controlling and why.
learnerActions: Present a draft investigation plan to a 'scientist' partner or mentor.
Respond to probing questions such as 'What else might be affecting your result?' and 'Which rival explanation does each control rule out?'
Revise the plan to remove hidden uncontrolled variables and to confirm the enquiry type fits the question.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating and defending a plan can surface hidden confounds and push the 'why control?' reasoning to become explicit.

constraints: Planning independence is the assessed step-up: move pupils from teacher-set to self-planned investigations where they decide the variables and enquiry type and justify their choices.
Require a 'why control?' justification for each controlled variable, tied to a specific rival explanation it rules out, not just a list of things kept the same.
Introduce input/output/kept-same (independent/dependent/control) language in child-friendly form as a bridge to KS3 vocabulary without over-formalising at this age.
A planning proforma (question → enquiry type → variable to change → to measure → to control → prediction → how to record) helps make the full plan visible before any doing.
Formal hypothesis wording, sample size and risk assessment belong to the later (KS3) tier, not here.

Categorisation and multiple-choice questions can check and consolidate variable-role and enquiry-type knowledge, while a labelled reference image can only illustrate or label it; neither elicits a learner constructing and running their own plan, so keep them as assessment or scaffold rather than the main teach.
A labelled reference image of variable types is a reference scaffold only — it cannot let the child construct and test a plan.

Experimental-design logic is not inherently spatial, so a 3D/spatial representation is not required here; its conceptual value for this skill is unestablished rather than categorically absent, and it should not be ruled out as harmful either.
Changing more than one variable at once is not a 'bigger/better' experiment — it prevents attributing the result to any single cause; keep exactly one input varied.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source marks the AKSIS over-default claim (fair-test-by-default) as unverified (verified:false); treat statements about pupils over-defaulting to fair testing — including the sourceClaims that cite it in activities 1 and 2 — as a reported finding, not confirmed here.

Legacy entries asserted that 'a static image cannot teach this', '3D adds no conceptual value', and that only the live planner makes control 'felt'. These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the sources; they have been softened to scoped affordance/limitation statements. A fixed image can still serve as a reference even though it cannot be manipulated.

The confounded-plant diagnostic (different light AND water AND pot size) is sound as written: the point is precisely that multiple simultaneous differences prevent attribution. Feedback wording states all three stated confounds consistently.

The original commonMisconception that 'more variables changed = a bigger/better experiment' was previously only addressed implicitly; it is now explicitly named in activity 1 so the substantive point is preserved.

probeDeeper: Which things must be kept the same here, and what alternative explanation does each one rule out?
If the sunny plant had the SAME water and pot and still grew taller, what could you now conclude?
Someone asks whether the class gets taller through the year — is a fair test the right enquiry, or would observing over time fit better?
Why does changing only one thing let us trust the answer, when changing several doesn't?
assess.correctAnswer: No — more than one thing differs (light, water, pot size), so you can't tell which caused the taller plant; the test is confounded. A strong response says you must keep water, pot size, soil, plant type and starting height the same, changing ONLY the light, so that any difference in growth can be attributed to light alone. It frames controlling variables as what makes the result VALID — it removes rival explanations — and may name this as a fair/comparative enquiry rather than, say, observation over time.

errorPatterns.pattern: Accepts the confounded conclusion: 'yes, it was the sunlight — the sunny one grew taller'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Highlight the two other differences (water, pot); ask which one caused it — establish that with three differences you can't tell.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Endorses the causal claim without noticing the extra differences.

errorPatterns.pattern: Rule without reason: knows to 'keep everything the same' but can't say why, or keeps irrelevant things constant while missing the real confounds.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Tie each control to a specific rival explanation it removes — control exists to make the cause attributable.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States the control rule but can't tie it to ruling out alternative causes, or mis-targets what to control.

errorPatterns.pattern: Fair-test-by-default (AKSIS): treats every question as a fair test even when observation-over-time or pattern-seeking would fit better.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Review the five enquiry types; match the question to the appropriate type before planning controls.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked about a different question type, still reaches for a fair test.

responseLevels.gap: Accepts the confounded conclusion, or recites 'keep things the same' without linking it to trusting the result.
responseLevels.full: Identifies the confounds, specifies which variables to control and why each removes a rival explanation, frames variable-control as what makes a conclusion valid, and matches the question to the appropriate enquiry type.
responseLevels.partial: Spots that more than one thing differs and knows to control variables, but can't fully justify why (in terms of ruling out alternative causes) or mis-selects the enquiry type.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A student wants to know if plants grow taller with more sunlight. They put one plant on a sunny windowsill and another in a dark cupboard — but they also water the sunny one more and use a bigger pot for it. After two weeks the sunny plant is taller. Can they be sure it was the sunlight? Talk me through what's wrong with the test, what needs to be kept the same, and why that matters for trusting the answer.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with the concept spots that several differences make the cause unknowable and justifies control in terms of ruling out alternative explanations. A child without it either declares the conclusion safe ('sunlight, obviously') or recites 'keep things the same' as a rule without connecting it to why the conclusion would otherwise be untrustworthy.
